title: Pride and Prejudice
synopsis: Longbourn, regency England. A single man in possession of a good fortune is in want of a wife. Your mother is, somehow, aware of every such man in the county.

nodes.text: The news reaches Longbourn before the tenant does: five thousand a year, a chaise and four, no wife. Your mother has the household inventoried by luncheon — which daughter in which gown, which neighbour might manage the introduction. Your father refuses to call on him for three days purely to watch her suffer, having already called on him Tuesday. He tells nobody. He is enjoying himself enormously.

choices.consequence: You let her run the entire campaign aloud over dinner and supply encouraging noises at intervals. It costs you one evening and buys Jane three weeks of quiet.
You ask innocently whether the gentleman might prefer a wife who reads. Her nerves are invoked, at volume, for the next forty minutes.

nodes.text: Bingley dances every dance, learns the names of the officers' sisters, and asks Jane twice. His friend stands against the wall with his hands behind his back and does not dance, does not speak, and surveys the room the way a man surveys a stack of unpaid bills. The figure goes round inside half an hour: ten thousand a year, and proud enough to make it a defect.

choices.consequence: You decide he is a specimen, and specimens are free. You watch him fail to enjoy himself and enjoy yourself considerably.
It goes in under a rib and stays there. You will spend nine months proving to a man that you never cared for his opinion.

nodes.text: He says it four feet from your chair, to Bingley, in the voice men use when they have forgotten that women occupy rooms: tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me. Charlotte hears it and goes carefully still. You laugh out loud, genuinely, and tell the story that night with the timing sharpened, and by Thursday half of Meryton has it word for word.

choices.consequence: You make it a joke you own, which is the only defence available, and you tell it so well that nobody notices you never let go of it.
You put the sentence somewhere cold and keep it. Every decent thing you later learn about the man must be dragged past it first.

nodes.text: Your mother refuses the carriage deliberately. She has read the sky, measured the mile and a half, and calculated that a soaking is worth a night beneath Bingley's roof. It works better than intended. Jane arrives wet and is put to bed with a fever and a throat she cannot swallow through, and your mother is delighted in a way nobody in the family finds it convenient to name.

choices.consequence: You leave before breakfast and cross three miles of ploughed field on foot, because a note said sore throat and you can read your sister's handwriting.
You wait for the carriage like a sensible woman and arrive clean and composed. Jane's face when you finally come in tells you what the extra hours cost.

nodes.text: You come in with six inches of Hertfordshire on your hem, your hair down, high colour from the walk. Miss Bingley waits until you are upstairs before she begins: the wildness of it, the conceit of independence, the petticoat. Darcy remarks that the exercise had brightened your eyes, then looks as though he has startled himself, and says almost nothing for the remainder of the evening.

choices.consequence: You never once mention the hem, which starves them, and Miss Bingley is obliged to raise the subject twice more herself to keep it breathing.
You apologise for the state of your skirts and watch her accept it like a small tax gratefully collected. You do not make that error twice.

nodes.text: He does it over cards, at the pianoforte, above a book whose pages have stopped turning. You assume it is cataloguing — a country girl, faults noted for later. So you go at him: teasing, contradicting, agreeing with things you do not believe to see what he will do. He answers seriously every single time, which ruins the sport and irritates you for reasons you decline to examine.

choices.consequence: You let no sentence of his stand unturned. He begins arranging to be in whichever room you are in, and you take this for surveillance.
You ask him one honest question about his sister and get four minutes of an entirely different man. You set the evidence aside as inconvenient.

nodes.text: He is a clergyman who quotes his patroness the way other men quote scripture, and he has come to choose a wife from among the daughters of the house he will inherit. He proposes in the breakfast room with the door shut, itemising his motives — the example to his parish, the express wishes of Lady Catherine — and explains that a lady's refusal is customary and need not be attended to.

choices.consequence: You say no four times in increasingly plain English. Your mother will not speak to you for a week, and your father cannot stop smiling into his coffee.
You come within one breath of yes — the house saved, the family provided for, your mother silenced — and the breath goes out as no. You will revisit that breath for years.

nodes.text: She is twenty-seven, plain by the county's accounting, and has spent years listening to her brothers calculate what she costs to keep. She accepts him within three days of your refusal and tells you herself, in the garden, steadily, before anyone else can get to you. She asks one thing: that you come and see the parsonage. She is not asking your approval. She is asking not to have to explain.

choices.consequence: You take her hand and promise March, and the effort of not saying the other thing is the first piece of grown work you have ever done.
Your face reaches it before your manners do, and she sees it. The friendship survives, and it is never quite the same shape again.

nodes.text: He wears regimentals, remembers your name, and arrives at precisely the grievance you were hoping somebody would confirm: a living promised by the late Mr Darcy and withheld by the son out of jealousy. He tells it beautifully, all in one go, to a woman he met an hour ago. That last detail is the entire case against him, and you will not notice it for six months.

choices.consequence: You believe him at once and completely, because he flatters your judgement by agreeing with it. Prejudice is not blindness; it is being told what you already decided.
You note that a stranger has handed you a rich man's private disgrace over one cup of tea. Then you file the doubt somewhere you do not look.

nodes.text: Charlotte has arranged the parsonage so that her husband's favourite sitting room faces the road, which keeps him at the window and out of her way. You admire the arrangement and say nothing whatever about it. At Rosings, Lady Catherine demands your age, your sisters' ages, whether your mother keeps a closed carriage, and how many instruments you play, then advises more practice on a piano you do not own.

choices.consequence: You answer everything civilly and let the woman have her room. Charlotte's eyes lift once from her plate in thanks, and that settles the account.
You tell her plainly that you decline to state your age, and the table stops breathing, and Mr Collins does not recover speech until the carriage home.

nodes.text: He comes in while you are alone with a headache, paces the room, and opens with how hard he has struggled against it — your family, your connections, the degradation of the entire business — then asks you to marry him like a man settling an account he has decided to honour. He fully expects yes. What is astonishing is that he is not being cruel. He believes he is being honest.

choices.consequence: You refuse him with Wickham's story and Jane's ruined autumn laid out one after the other, and you have never been so articulate or so wrong about half your evidence.
For one second the house, the library and the man's plain wretchedness all arrive together and you nearly — and then he mentions your family again.

nodes.text: He puts it into your hand in the grove at eight in the morning and walks off without waiting. Two sheets, written through the night, close on both sides. Jane's apparent indifference, which he read wrongly and says so. Then Wickham: the living taken in cash, three thousand pounds spent in two years, and Georgiana at Ramsgate, fifteen years old, stopped four days before the elopement.

choices.consequence: You read it four times on a single walk and your whole understanding of the past year comes apart in your hands. Until this hour you had never known yourself.
You mean to burn it. You carry it home in your pocket instead, and it is still there at supper, and it will sit in a drawer for the rest of your life.

nodes.text: Your aunt wants to see the house, and you confirm twice that the family is away before agreeing. The grounds have not been bullied into shape; the stream is left where the stream was. Indoors, a housekeeper who has known him since he was four says he is the best master and best landlord she ever served, in the tone of a woman with no reason to flatter tourists.

choices.consequence: You stand at a window above the valley and permit yourself the arithmetic — all this might have been mine — and you are honest enough to be ashamed and honest enough not to stop.
You make a joke to your aunt about the size of the trout stream. It lands flat, and you hear yourself hearing it.

nodes.text: He comes round the corner of his own house twenty yards off, a day early, in riding clothes, and you both go scarlet. Then he does the thing you have no defence against: asks after your parents, walks your uncle down to the water to talk about fishing, and requests — carefully, as though it might be refused — leave to present his sister. He never mentions the letter. Not once, ever.

choices.consequence: You sustain a quarter of an hour of ordinary talk about roads and weather, and it costs you more than the refusal at Hunsford ever did.
You answer two questions wrongly and one of them twice. He is patient about it, and the patience is far worse than mockery.

nodes.text: The letters reach you at the inn with Darcy standing in the room. Sixteen years old, gone from Brighton with him, and Colonel Forster has traced the pair as far as London and no further — which means no Scotland, no licence, no intention. You say it aloud because you cannot hold it in your mouth. He goes white, crosses the room twice, and leaves without explaining himself.

choices.consequence: You are in a carriage within the hour, composing across every mile what you will say to Jane. None of it survives contact with her face at the door.
You keep your voice level the whole way into Hertfordshire for your aunt's sake, and only unclench behind a shut door, and only then notice your hands.

nodes.text: He finds them in a boarding house off Edward Street. He bargains with a man he despises, settles a thousand pounds and the commission and every debt, stands up in the church himself, and swears the whole party to secrecy — because he holds the business to be his own fault for keeping Wickham's character private. Your uncle takes the credit. Your aunt then writes you five pages she was not supposed to write.

choices.consequence: You work it out from one slip in her letter, and the gratitude arrives with something underneath it that you are not yet prepared to name.
You believe the family version and thank the wrong man warmly. There is a certain peace in that, and it lasts nine days.

nodes.text: She arrives at Longbourn unannounced, refuses refreshment, inspects the sitting room as though pricing it, and marches you out among the trees to report that a rumour of the most alarming nature has reached her. Contradict it. Then: promise me. She lists her objections in order — his cousin, the arts, his mother's wishes — and never once considers that the person she ought to be threatening is not you.

choices.consequence: You decline politely four times. She leaves furious and repeats every syllable to her nephew, which informs him that you did not say no. Her interference makes the match.
You give her a soft answer to get her out of the shrubbery, then stand among the wet leaves despising yourself for the softness.

nodes.text: You get outdoors together for the first time in a year and walk the lane toward the mount without either of you appearing to steer it. You thank him for Lydia. He says he thought only of you. Then, quietly, with no reference to your relations or his own consequence: his affections are unchanged, and one word from you ends the subject permanently.

choices.consequence: You say yes on a public road in daylight, and he cannot look at you, and spends the next mile saying things he has evidently been rehearsing since April.
You make yourself say it aloud first — that you were wrong, comprehensively, and knew it in a grove at eight in the morning — before you let yourself say yes.

nodes.text: She sits perfectly still for a full minute, which has not happened in your lifetime. Then: ten thousand a year, and pin money, and jewels, and a house in town, and what will Jane's be, and had she not always said there was something in his face. She has spent a year calling him the most disagreeable man in England. Not one syllable of that year is ever mentioned again by anybody.

choices.consequence: You let her run, and count the roses in the ceiling plaster, and think about a man walking out of a grove without waiting for a reply.
You take her hands, get her sitting, get something sweet into her, and she grips your fingers — and for a moment she is only a frightened woman with five daughters.

nodes.text: Two brides, one aisle, and your father giving away half his household before noon. Bingley is so happy he keeps glancing at the congregation as if to share it around. Darcy says his part quietly and exactly, and only Jane, standing nearest, sees his hand move on the book. Mr Collins sends a letter of congratulation containing four cautions, one scriptural warning, and a veiled complaint about the seating.

choices.consequence: You take his hand at the church door and feel the grip come harder than the occasion requires. It is the most he will ever say in public.
You reach for your sister before your husband, in front of the whole parish, and Darcy waits without a flicker of minding — which is the moment you are certain.

nodes.text: The library took two generations to buy and the ladder runs on a brass rail the length of the room. He shows you which shelves are his father's and which are his, and you notice the newest run is novels, which he did not previously own. Georgiana watches the two of you argue about one of them, looks alarmed, then delighted, then permanently emboldened.

choices.consequence: You claim the chair by the north window so completely that within a year the servants have learned not to dust that end of the room before noon.
You learn the tenants, the drainage and the accounts, and the housekeeper quietly stops saying poor Mr Darcy, alone in this great house.
There is a further version in which you keep the ladder, the window and the argument, and add one locked drawer with paper in it.

nodes.text: You run the place properly: tenants known by name, the school roof rebuilt, the household accounts in your own hand. The Darcy children inherit their father's silences and your mouth, which the county finds difficult to manage. Lady Catherine holds out three years, then arrives without warning, inspects the drawing room, pronounces one chimney-piece adequate, and stays a fortnight. No apology is offered or requested. She returns every spring, and complains about the roads.

Jane settles thirty miles off and you are in one another's houses constantly, cousins underfoot in both. The children cannot reliably say whose mother is whose. Well into middle age the two of you still go helpless in a sitting room over nothing — a look, a phrase your mother used to use — while your husbands stand in the doorway wearing an expression they have privately agreed never to discuss. She has never said an unkind word about anyone. You have said them for her.

You begin with the marriage market of one small county and discover you cannot stop. It goes out anonymously, by a lady, and the reviews call it a pleasant trifle concerning nothing very much. Your family reads it aloud in the evenings without recognising a single soul in it. Your husband recognises everybody, says so exactly once, and never again — then quietly buys the second edition in a quantity that embarrasses the bookseller.
